The job you do by hand every week
SENT Tue 01 Sep 2026 46 recipients · 6 unique opens
Proposed repost date: Wed 09 Sep 2026
LinkedIn post, ready to paste 
Pick the one job you do by hand every week. Not the biggest one. The one that keeps coming back.

Now put a clock on it. Time it start to finish, the next time you sit down to do it. Do not estimate, because your estimate will be wrong in a specific direction. Work you do on autopilot never arrives as a bill. It arrives four minutes here and twenty there, spread so thin across a week that it never looks like the thing to fix.

That number is the whole argument. Not a statistic about AI. Not a case study from a company that looks nothing like yours. Your number, for your job, measured once.

Last week I wrote about the conversations that go cold while you are busy. This is the same problem wearing different clothes. Both are cheap to ignore in any single week and expensive over a year, and neither one ever announces itself.

I found my own version of this by admitting it in front of you a few weeks ago. My problem was never building the thing. It was getting anyone to look at it once it existed. What fixed it was not motivation. It was putting the job on a repeating schedule with a date attached, the same way I would have handled it if it belonged to somebody else.

Here is why I keep pointing people at a weekly job instead of a big one.

It repeats, so whatever you fix pays you back every week rather than once. You already know every step, which means there is nothing to design, and design is where most of these attempts die. And it is small enough to finish in one sitting. That last part matters more than it sounds. A half-built automation is worse than none, because now you have a thing you do not trust and still have to check.

Most owners do the opposite. They go looking for one tool that will handle everything, and everything is too big to describe, so the tool gets configured for a week and abandoned. One repeating job fits in a paragraph. That is the entire difference between the two approaches, and it has nothing to do with which tool you picked.

One warning, because this is the part people get backwards. Do not automate the job you hate. Hate is a feeling and it is a bad selector. The job you hate might happen twice a year. Automate the job that repeats, even if you do not mind doing it, because repetition is arithmetic and arithmetic is the only thing here that compounds.

So: one job, one clock, this week. If the number surprises you, you have found your first one. If it does not, you have spent four minutes and can stop reading me on this subject.

The most valuable thing AI does in my business is remember

The most valuable thing AI does in my business is remember.

That is not where I started. I pointed it at the work you can see, the scheduling and the back office and the outreach. Useful, all of it. None of it was the thing costing me money.

What cost me money was quieter, and I have told you about it before. I had a process that could sort and score incoming work perfectly well, and then nothing happened, because the result landed in a queue I never opened. The machine did its job. I was the broken part. There was no alarm for that, because nothing had failed.

Look at your own week and you will find the same shape. A quote nobody chased. A reply that got read and never answered. And somewhere in there, a promise to circle back that has aged past the point where circling back is comfortable. None of it feels like a crisis. It feels like a normal busy week. And it is the most expensive habit in a small business, because every one of those people had already raised their hand. You already paid to get them there.

In my old life in HR, nothing about a person was allowed to just sit. Every case had an owner and a date, and if the date passed, somebody heard about it. Almost nobody thinks to point that same discipline at their own sales conversations, which is strange, because that is where the money sits.

So that is what I built. Every conversation has a next date attached to it. If I said I would follow up, something is watching for that date whether or not I am. If someone replies, I know that day. If a thread goes quiet past a certain point, it comes back and asks me what I want to do about it. Nothing clever in any of it, no impressive model, just a boring set of rules that runs while I am not looking.

Here is why I would build this before almost anything else. Chasing a new audience is a bet on somebody you have not met. Following up is a near certainty with somebody who already told you they were interested. One of those has a known cost and the other is a guess.

One warning, because I got this part wrong first. A follow-up system only helps if it is honest about what happened. If it marks something done because a message went out, rather than because a human came back, you have built a machine whose only real skill is reassuring you. That is worse than nothing, because now you believe it. Sent is not answered. Make it prove the answer.

One move this week, no software required. Open the last thirty days of your email and find every conversation where you spoke last and the other person never came back. Do not build anything yet. Count them. That number is your leak, and you cannot fix a leak you have not measured.

Then take the most valuable one on that list and write to that person today. The system comes later, and it is much easier to build once you know what it is protecting.

I shipped a paid product this week. Idea to live to taking payments, in an afternoon.

Almost nobody saw it.

I only said the real problem out loud when I got frustrated with my own operation. I do not have a problem creating things and making them go live. I have a problem getting people to see what I have created.

I spent years in HR watching process people hunt for the one step that limits everything, fix that step, and leave the rest alone. Then I spent a year building, and I noticed I had been polishing steps that were never the constraint. The real constraint was distribution.

Building feels like progress. Asking someone to look feels like asking a favor, so distribution loses the fight for my time almost every time I put the two side by side.

Building has a finish line. You know the exact minute the page goes live. Being seen has no finish line, so it loses when you can only do one.

Here is the rule I am writing down for myself, in public, so it is harder to skip again: a page is not finished when it is live. It is finished when there is a plan for who sees it, with names or dates attached to that plan.

Look at your own last week. What did you build, fix, or launch that nobody outside your head saw? Do not answer that in your head. Go find the actual thing, then hit reply and tell me what it was.

The same problem is probably sitting in your business right now.

Most small businesses have no file anywhere that tells an AI assistant what they sell, who buys it, and what they charge. The business is real. It is just not written down anywhere the AI can reach. So when someone asks ChatGPT or Claude for a recommendation in that category, the AI is guessing, and it usually guesses wrong or skips the business completely. Same shape as my problem. You built the thing and nobody can see it.

I ran the in-person version of this in Sandy on July 30. People came, built the file in the room, and more have been asking since, which is why the next one is online. Next Wednesday, August 19th, 11am to noon Mountain time.

You bring a laptop and an hour. You leave with three things: the file itself, written in your own words and running on your own machine, the recipes to keep using it after we hang up, and a cheat sheet built to print.

You cannot fire your way to an AI win
SENT Mon 03 Aug 2026 32 recipients · 6 unique opens
Proposed repost date: Thu 17 Sep 2026
LinkedIn post, ready to paste 
The assumption I keep seeing is that AI lets you cut people and pocket the difference. That math rarely survives contact with reality.

Here is what actually happens. A team hands a function to a model. The model handles most cases cleanly. The rest need judgment, context, and the memory of the person who just got let go. Now your operations lead is doing the work the model could not, with none of the original context, and customers are feeling the gap.

I run my own business with AI doing a lot of what I used to do by hand, so I know how it actually goes. Nobody got cut to make my setup exist. The work AI does for me is work I could not do at all before. Outreach at the volume of a small team. Back-office tasks that used to eat my evenings. Checks that catch mistakes before they cost me a weekend.

The expansion story is more honest than the replacement story. AI lets one operator hold ground that used to need a team. It does not let a team shrink by the same headcount and still produce the same output. The arithmetic is not symmetrical, and that is the whole point.

Why does the replacement story keep getting told? It sells consulting, and it gives an executive a clean number for a slide. Fire a group, save the salary, deploy the model, call it transformation. What the slide leaves out is the long tail the model cannot handle, the team quietly absorbing it, and the customer experience slipping while the savings and the costs sit on two different ledgers.

AI is not a cheaper version of headcount. It is a different kind of capacity. The operators who treat it that way keep their people and grow their reach at the same time. The ones who treat it as headcount math end up paying for the model, paying the consultant, and paying their team overtime to cover what the model dropped.

The framing is the strategy. Everything after it is consequence.

That is the work I do at Catalyst Works. I help owners find where AI actually fits, without getting burned. If that is the season you are in, come say hello: catalystworks.consulting

The four questions I score before I automate anything
SENT Mon 27 Jul 2026 30 recipients · 5 unique opens
Proposed repost date: Wed 30 Sep 2026
LinkedIn post, ready to paste 
One of my automations ran 880 times before I noticed it had produced nothing.

Green logs. Moving queue. Blank output, every single run, because the source it pulled from had quietly blocked it from day one. Nothing failed loudly, and that was exactly the problem. An automation you trust is an automation you stop watching.

That incident is why nothing in my operation gets automated anymore until it survives four questions:

Frequency. How often does the job repeat? Daily beats weekly beats monthly. Repetition is where a handoff compounds.

Time drain. How much of the week does it actually eat? Count the small interruptions, they are the expensive part.

Rules-clarity. Could you write the steps down so a new hire could follow them? A job that lives only in your head is not ready to hand to a machine.

Stakes if rough. If the output came back eighty percent right, is that a quick fix or a damaged client relationship? Your first workflow should be one where a near-miss is cheap.

Score your candidate jobs, five points each, twenty max. The winner is almost never the exciting idea. It is the boring job you could write the manual for. That is what makes it buildable this week.

A tool is a thing you open. A workflow is a thing that runs. Go build one that earns the trust before it gets the keys.

AI exposes broken handoffs. It will not fix them.

Buying AI before you fix your workflow is like bolting a bigger engine onto a car with no steering.

The bottleneck is almost never the tool. It lives in the seam between two owners. Sales to onboarding. A draft to a reviewer. A finished task to whoever ships it. That is where work disappears, where context dies, and where AI exposes the gap the loudest.

I learned this the hard way in my own business. I had a process that could sort and score incoming work perfectly well. And then nothing happened, because the result landed in a queue I never opened. The handoff from the machine back to me was the whole bottleneck. The model was not the problem. The seam was.

What fixed it was not a smarter model. It was a simple alert on my phone with one button, and a way to actually close the loop when a task was done. Small, boring pieces. Zero new AI.

Most teams drop an AI tool into a broken process and call the broken process a strategy. The tool exposes every gap. It closes none of them. That part is your job.

Here is how to find the broken handoff before AI finds it for you. Walk one task end to end. Not the clean version. The real one. Where does it pause? Who is waiting on whom? Where does a status sit stale for more than a day? That is your seam.

Fix the seam first. Then add the engine. In that order, every time.

Your AI is pointed at the wrong link.
SENT Thu 11 Jun 2026 3 recipients · 1 unique opens

LinkedIn post, ready to paste 
Hey friend,

Growing up in Conakry, the power cut out most days. The surges and outages killed appliances constantly, and replacing them cost money we did not have. So you learned to open the thing up, find the one part that had actually failed, and fix that part. Not the whole machine. The broken piece. New things were expensive. Diagnosis was free.

I think about that every time I watch someone buy another AI tool.

A leader wires a shiny new model into the process they already run, and waits. Six months later the team is frustrated, the number has not moved, and everyone blames the model.

The model is usually fine. The map is wrong.

Every operation is a chain. Work flows from one step to the next, and somewhere in that chain one link does all the waiting: a handoff where work piles up, a step where the customer quietly gives up. Eli Goldratt called that link the constraint, and he showed something most people never quite believe. The constraint is the only place where improvement moves the whole system. Fix anywhere else and you are polishing a link that was never the problem.

AI does not change that math. It amplifies whatever you point it at.

Which means a wrongly aimed AI is not neutral. It is worse than what you had before, because now the stuck system runs faster and looks productive.

Point it at the constraint and you get real speed. Point it at a link that was already fine and you get a faster version of the same stuck system. And if the process was broken before AI ever arrived, you get confident garbage, delivered quicker than before.

A couple of weeks ago I wrote about building your own setup instead of buying another course. This is the other half of that letter. The setup is worthless if you aim it at the wrong link.

So here is the one question. Ask it before any tool, any automation, any purchase. Answer it without naming a single piece of technology:

## Where does work wait the longest before it moves?

Not where people look busy, and not where it feels slow. Where the work itself sits, untouched, before someone picks it up and carries it forward. That is your constraint. That is where AI belongs. Everything else is expensive decoration.

It is the same instinct from that house in Conakry with no power, moved into a company with a budget. The instinct travels. The price tag is the only thing that changes.

This week: pick one process your team runs more than twice a week. Walk it end to end, slowly, and find where it stops. Then point your attention there, before you point your money anywhere. Diagnosis is still free.

Next week, the link nobody draws on the map: the people who have to use the thing you just bought.

Until next week,

Boubacar

Before You Buy Another AI Tool, Read This
SENT Wed 29 Apr 2026 2 recipients · 1 unique opens
Proposed repost date: Wed 21 Oct 2026
LinkedIn post, ready to paste 
Hey friend,

You saw a demo. You got excited. You bought the tool. And now six months later you are paying for software your team barely uses.

That is the pattern. It is playing out across companies right now, and it is costing people real money.

Here is how it happens. Someone hears about AI and goes looking for what to apply it to. Suddenly every problem in the business looks like it could be solved by an AI tool. The hiring process. The customer support backlog. The reporting. The onboarding. Pick your pain point and there is a vendor ready to sell you the AI solution for it.

The problem is not the excitement. The problem is starting with the tool and working backwards to the problem. When you do that, you skip the one step that actually matters: figuring out what is broken and why.

Let's Also Name What AI Actually Is

A lot of what gets sold as AI right now is not AI. It is automation. Rule-based logic. If-this-then-that workflows with a language model bolted on for the pitch deck.

That is not a criticism of automation. Automation is genuinely useful. But if you are paying AI prices for automation value, and skipping the root cause work that would tell you which one you actually need, you are getting hit twice.

What the Numbers Actually Tell You

More than 80% of AI projects fail. That is twice the failure rate of regular IT projects. And 48% of C-suite executives now call AI adoption a "massive disappointment" on ROI, up from 34% just last year.

But here is what those numbers do not say: most of those projects were not killed by bad AI. They were killed by processes that were already broken before the AI showed up. The AI just made the failure more expensive and more visible.

If your customer support team is overwhelmed because your product has a confusing onboarding flow, an AI chatbot does not fix that. It automates the confusion. If your sales reporting is a mess because nobody agreed on definitions three years ago, an AI analytics layer does not fix that.

It just produces faster wrong answers.

One Thing to Do This Week

Before you greenlight any new AI purchase, answer this question without mentioning technology: what exact problem am I solving, and why does it exist?

If you cannot answer that clearly, you are not ready to buy. You are ready to diagnose.

That is where the real work starts. Reply to this email and tell me what you are trying to solve. I read every reply.

Until next week,
Boubacar

THE VERDICT

Your revenue grew. Your margin did not. The problem is not your pricing. It is the
person whose name appears on every deliverable before it goes to the client.

That person is probably you.

THE SCENE

Picture this:

Professional services firm. Eight people. Three years of 20% growth.

The owner had done everything right. Hired carefully. Built a process. Brought in a
project manager specifically to take things off his plate.

Margin: flat for two years.

He had already raised rates. Twice. Nothing moved.

One question cuts through it: who reviewed the last five deliverables before they
went to the client?

The answer is almost always the same.

"Me."

"Every one?"

"Every one."

He was not a control freak. His team had simply learned to wait. His review was the
gate. His calendar was the bottleneck. The business had grown around him without
anyone noticing that he hadn't.

THE MECHANISM

Here is what this looks like from inside.

Revenue grows. The owner's available hours do not. Work piles up behind the one
person whose sign-off the whole system requires. The team finishes at full speed.
Then they wait. Projects that are 95% complete sit in a queue until a window opens.
The window comes late. The client feels it. The delay gets absorbed into delivery
time. Margin takes the hit.

Nobody names it because it does not look like a structural problem. It looks like a
busy owner. The accountant sees a growing revenue line with a flat margin and
suggests raising rates. The coach sees stress and suggests delegation. The project
manager builds a better tracker.

None of it works. You cannot organize your way out of a capacity constraint. You can
only move it.

This is not a character flaw. It is a system that was never designed to run without
you. The fix is to design it so it can.

That means two things. First: define what a finished deliverable looks like in
writing, with enough specificity that someone other than you can make the call.
Second: give someone the authority to make it.

That is not a loss of control. It is the difference between standards that live in
your head and standards that live in a document anyone can apply.

THE TELL

Pull your last ten client deliverables. For each one, write down who touched it
before it went out.

Count how many have your name.

If the answer is more than half, you are the constraint. The question is not whether
your standards are too high. The question is whether anyone else knows what they are.

THE SIGNAL

This is one of the most predictable structural problems in professional services
firms that have grown past their first three years. It rarely gets named. Owners
feel the pressure. They hire into it. They raise rates around it. The constraint
stays.

Reply and tell me what your number is. I read every one.

If you know an operator who suspects the problem is structural but cannot name it,
forward this. That is the whole pitch.

Boubacar Barry
Catalyst Works Consulting | catalystworks.consulting

Most consultants bring frameworks. I bring a diagnosis.

Most owners never ask for help with AI, and it is not because they think they have it handled.

It is because nobody has ever told them what they would be buying. Consulting gets sold as a noun. Strategy. Transformation. Enablement. You cannot picture any of that, so you cannot picture asking for it, so you do not.

So here is the shape of the thing I built, plainly, including the price and including how it ends.

The first month is the heaviest. We find the one constraint that is costing you money, which is almost never the thing you would have guessed, and we fix that one. Not a roadmap of eleven things. One, running, in your business, on your systems.

Months two and three we do the same again, and I start handing the work over while it is still small enough to hand over.

By months four to six the point is that your own people are running it and I am mostly answering questions. From month seven the plan is that you drop a tier, hand it to a permanent hire, or stop.

That is written down before you start, and it is the part I would want to read if I were the one buying.

Most retainers are built to grow. This one is built to shrink.

I want to be honest about why, because it is not generosity. A retainer that grows has to keep finding reasons to exist, and eventually those reasons stop being about you. I spent years in HR watching capable teams get replaced by a dependency on somebody outside the building, and I am not interested in being that.

What you own at the end is the whole point. The systems run on your accounts, not mine. Your team knows how they work, because they were the ones being taught while it was built. The instructions are written down in your words, so a new hire can pick them up. If I disappeared, none of it stops.

The scale starts at $2,500 a month and the main rung is $5,000, depending on how much of me you need. I put the numbers on the page rather than making you ask, because making you ask is a tactic and I do not like being on the receiving end of it.

One more thing, and I would rather you hear it from me than work it out.

I have not had this conversation with anyone yet. I built the offer, wrote the step-down, and set the prices before having a single one of these on the books, and I am telling you the shape of it now rather than after it is safe. That is the same thing I have been doing in front of you all year. If you would rather wait until I have a wall of logos, that is a completely reasonable way to buy and I will not be offended.

If you would rather be early, the whole thing is written out, step-down and prices included, and you can book a 20-minute call from that page: catalystworks.consulting/fx/nl

Bring the one problem you have not been able to fix. Twenty minutes, nothing to prepare, and if it is not the kind of problem this is built for I will say so and point you somewhere better.

If you would rather not book anything yet, just reply to this email with that one problem instead. Same answer, no calendar.

And if this is not for you but a name came to mind while you were reading, that name is the single most useful thing you can send me today. Someone running a company of ten to fifty people who keeps saying they should be doing something about all this. You do not need to introduce us. Just tell me who they are and I will take it from there.

The AI thing you tried that did not work

You tried it. It gave you something generic and slightly wrong. You closed the tab and got on with your day, and somewhere in the back of your head it filed itself under "not for us".

I want to make the case that you were right to close the tab and wrong about the conclusion.

Here is what almost certainly happened. You asked it to do a piece of real work in your business, and you gave it none of the things you would have given a new hire on their first morning. It did not know what you sell, who buys it, what you charge, who you are not for, or how you talk. So it did the only thing left available to it, which was to write the average version of your industry. Generic and slightly wrong is exactly what that produces. It is not a sign of a weak tool. It is a sign of a tool with no information.

Think about how absurd the equivalent would be with a person. You would not hand a new hire a customer email on day one, tell them nothing about the business, and then conclude from the result that hiring does not work for companies like yours.

Four things fix most of it, and none of them are technical.

Tell it what you sell, in the words your customers use rather than the words on your website. Tell it who your good customer is and, more usefully, who is a bad fit. Your prices go in too, including what you will not discount. Then give it two or three examples of work you were happy with, so it has something to copy that sounds like you rather than like the industry.

Write that down once, keep it somewhere you can paste from, and put it in front of the tool before you ask for anything. That is the whole fix. It takes an afternoon at most and it is the difference between generic and useful.

Now the part most owners have not thought about, and it is the one costing money.

The same gap works in reverse. When somebody asks an AI assistant to recommend a business like yours, it is answering from whatever it can find about you. If your business is not written down anywhere it can reach, it guesses, and it often guesses somebody else. You are not being beaten there. You are not in the room.

Everything above you can do on your own this week, and you should. The one thing you cannot do from your own desk is see what the machines already say about you, because you cannot un-know your own business well enough to read your site the way a stranger's assistant reads it.

So I built a free scan that does it for you. It reads your site the way an AI assistant would and shows you what it can and cannot work out about your business. About a minute, nothing to install, no call: catalystworks.consulting/scan

Look at the gaps it finds. Those gaps are the same four things above. Fix them for the machines and you will have fixed them for the tool on your own desk at the same time, which is the part I did not expect when I started doing this.

And if you read the result and think you would rather not be the one to sort it out, hit reply and tell me what it said. I read every one.

What to automate second
SCHEDULED for Mon 28 Sep 2026, not sent yet Nothing to repost until it sends. It is listed so the queue is the whole picture, not just the backlog.
LinkedIn post, ready to paste 
Your first AI tool is working. That is usually when it starts going wrong.

For weeks this newsletter has been about that first thing. Time the job you do by hand. Build one tool for it. Get it running.

That is the easy half.

The second one is where it goes wrong, and nobody sells a course on that part.

Here is the shape it takes. The first tool works. You got real hours back and you can feel it. So you go looking for the next one, and now everything qualifies: the inbox, the quotes, the scheduling, the follow-ups nobody makes. You pick three, start all three, and a couple of months later none of them are finished while the first one is still the only thing running.

The instinct that won you the first one is the same instinct that costs you the second.

When I was in the corporate world, the work was almost always the same job wearing a different suit. Find the one constraint that is actually costing the money. It is almost never the thing anyone points at first. Then you fix it, and something happens that nobody warns you about. The constraint does not disappear. It moves.

AI is no different. The moment your first tool takes a job off your plate, the thing limiting your week is somewhere else. It has to be. You changed the system.

So the second thing to automate is not the next item on your list. It is whatever became the bottleneck once the first one stopped being it.

That reads as obvious. It is not what anyone does. What people do is go back to the list they wrote before the first tool existed, a list that describes a business that no longer runs that way.

The practical version is short. Run the first tool for two weeks and leave the list alone. Then, at the end of an ordinary week, ask what you ran out of. Hours, attention, a person, or an answer you could not get fast enough. Whatever you ran out of is the second job. Build for that one.

Two weeks is not a number I can prove. It is just long enough for the new shape of your week to show up, and short enough that you have not lost interest.

The businesses that end up with an AI setup worth having did not build a lot of things. They built one thing, watched what changed, and then built the next right thing.

Slowly is a strategy.

If you would rather have someone run that loop with you than hand you a longer list, that is what a fractional engagement is for: catalystworks.consulting/fx/nl

How this page works

The loop this page closes. An issue sends on Monday. The Wednesday after, the Money Map reminds you to repost it. You open this page from that reminder, copy the body, download the image, post it, tick the box and set the date. The backlog shrinks by one and the count on this page is the truth about where you are.

What each control does

  • Download image saves the header straight to your Downloads folder. It is the real asset that shipped with the issue, at full size, not a screenshot of it.
  • Copy takes the whole post, body plus one line pointing back at the original issue. Nothing was rewritten or shortened; the words are the words that sent.
  • Done on LinkedIn moves the card to the Done column and writes the decision.
  • Posted on records the real date. It is separate from the tick on purpose, because you will sometimes tick it the day after you posted.
  • Your notes stay available whatever the status, including on ones you skip.

A card only counts as done once the database says so. If the banner at the top of the page is red, the numbers on this page are not to be trusted until it clears.

Proposed order for the backlog

This is a proposal. Nothing here is scheduled, and nothing fires on its own. Change any row by just doing it on a different day; the page records what actually happened, not what was planned.

Four rules built it, in this order:

  1. Newest first. Last week’s issue is worth more reposted than April’s.
  2. Two a week, Wednesday and Thursday. That is the standing cadence, and it clears the 12-issue backlog without a single day where you are posting three things.
  3. Nothing on 23 or 24 September. Those two days belong to the workshop push, and a repost competing with it wastes both.
  4. Reposts sit behind live campaigns, never in front of them. Where a date already carries a campaign, it is flagged rather than silently moved, because that is your call.

The Content Board, and what is not automatic yet

What you asked for was the tick here to update the Content Board by itself. Here is exactly where that stands, without dressing it up.

Every card links straight to its Content Board row, which is the fallback you named yourself, and it is live on this page today. Exact row links were resolved by an audit and are baked into every card.

The automatic push is NOT built. Saying otherwise would be the easy lie, so here is the real state. A proven write path into the board does exist for a different job — scripts/sync_content_review_approvals_to_notion.py has been pushing review-page approvals in since August, idempotently. It does not do this job, and pointing it at this page would actively corrupt the board, so it has been hard-blocked from this page rather than left as a trap. A dedicated syncer has not been written.

And a review pass found something worth more than that syncer. Ticking a box here still depends on you remembering to come to this page. When you repost from your phone and never open it, the board goes stale again and this page tells you something is still owed when it is not. The fix for that is not a button on this page. It is that sending should write to the board by itself — a Beehiiv webhook for sends, which is an afternoon of work and would make the board genuinely reliable rather than reliable-if-everyone-remembers.

So the honest sequence is: use the links today, and decide whether the webhook gets built. That is the one open question, and it is yours.

Worth knowing

Things worth knowing about this page, stated plainly.

  • Nothing on this page posts anything. No LinkedIn call, no Beehiiv call, no send. Every post is yours to make.
  • Two header images were made rather than recovered. The April 21 and June 17 issues shipped with Beehiiv’s stock placeholder, so there was no original to recover. Both cards are built from the locked template and both say so on the card.
  • The bodies are extracted from what Beehiiv actually sent, with the subscribe and footer furniture removed and nothing else touched. If a paragraph reads oddly, compare it against the live issue link on the card before assuming the extraction dropped something.
  • The four scheduled issues cannot be ticked until they send. The checkbox is disabled rather than hidden, so the queue reads as one list.
